title: Trump Chose a Naval Blockade When Iran Talks Broke Down
description_short: Trump Chose a Naval Blockade When Iran Talks Broke Down
description_medium: After 21 hours of U.S.-Iran talks in Islamabad ended without agreement on April 12, 2026, President Donald Trump announced a U.S. blockade of the Strait of Hormuz. Iran warned that a blockade would violate the ceasefire. Trump also threatened strikes on water-treatment facilities, power plants, and bridges if Iran did not abandon its nuclear program.
description_long: On April 12, 2026, after 21 hours of U.S.-Iran peace negotiations in Islamabad ended without agreement, Donald Trump announced that the United States would blockade the Strait of Hormuz. Vice President JD Vance led the U.S. delegation; he said Iran would not give up the possibility of developing nuclear weapons, while Iranian representatives said Washington needed to do more to earn their trust. Trump also threatened to bomb Iranian water-treatment facilities, power plants, and bridges unless Tehran abandoned its nuclear program. Iran warned that the announced blockade would breach the ceasefire. The next day, the Associated Press reported that the U.S. military had blockaded Iranian ports, documenting action beyond the initial announcement. The episode joined a breakdown in diplomacy with a naval operation and a separate threat against critical infrastructure. The available reports establish the blockade and the stated nuclear dispute, but do not describe its duration or final effect on shipping. This was a realized military measure following failed talks, not only a proposal.
notes: Repair note: Replaced the populated medium text to remove unsupported motive language and state the announced and reported blockade actions.

title: Death Penalty Massive Expansion - Federal Execution Acceleration and Capital Crime Increases
description_short: Death Penalty Massive Expansion - Federal Execution Acceleration and Capital Crime Increases
description_medium: The Thurgood Marshall Institute’s analysis of Project 2025 says the blueprint calls on the Justice Department to carry out executions of people already on federal death row and to expand the offenses eligible for capital punishment. The source describes a proposal, not an implemented Justice Department directive.
description_long: The Thurgood Marshall Institute’s analysis of Project 2025 describes a proposed expansion of federal capital punishment. It says the blueprint calls on the Justice Department to do “everything possible” to execute people already on federal death row and to broaden the number of cases that qualify for a death sentence. The analysis characterizes the plan as an extremely punitive approach and says it would pursue the expansion until Congress changed the law. It also argues that the proposed policy conflicts with Supreme Court precedent and discusses racial disparities in capital sentencing, including the separate case of Duane Buck. That example illustrates the institute’s concern about how race can enter death-penalty decisions; it is not evidence that a Trump administration directive changed Buck’s case. The source concerns Project 2025’s recommendations, not a Justice Department order or a completed increase in executions. It does not establish that Trump directed DOJ to carry out all federal death sentences or expanded capital eligibility on January 20, 2025. The proposal and the alleged implementation are distinct events.
subcategory: State-Sanctioned Killing Expansion and Racial Discrimination
notes: Needs context: The linked LDF analysis attributes these directives to Project 2025 recommendations, not to a Trump administration order. The entry’s January 20, 2025 date and the original long description present a proposal as an implemented expansion.

Proposed correction: Retain the Project 2025 recommendations as a proposal with the blueprint’s date, or provide a dated DOJ directive and implementation record before attributing execution acceleration or expanded eligibility to Trump’s administration.
Repair note: Replaced the populated long draft’s implementation claims with the source-supported policy proposal and its attribution.

title: Fred Trump Arrested Following KKK Brawl with Police
description_short: Fred Trump Arrested Following KKK Brawl with Police
description_medium: Contemporary reporting identifies Fred Trump, Donald Trump’s father, among men arrested after a Memorial Day 1927 clash between police and Ku Klux Klan marchers in Queens. He was not charged. The available historical accounts document the arrest, but do not establish that Fred Trump was a Klan member or determine his role in the confrontation.
description_long: On May 30, 1927, a Ku Klux Klan rally in Queens ended in a clash between marchers and police. Contemporary newspaper coverage reported that seven men, including 21-year-old Fred Trump, were arrested during or after the confrontation and later arraigned. TrumpFile’s historical account says Fred Trump escaped charges and notes that the available records do not establish whether he was a Klan member or merely present at the rally. The arrest is a documented historical event; it does not by itself show that he belonged to the organization or took part in the violence. Later accounts have also raised disputes over whether he wore Klan robes. The entry concerns Donald Trump’s father, not Donald Trump’s own conduct, and the record does not support claims that the 1927 event determined his son’s later politics. Keeping those distinctions clear allows the arrest to be described without turning proximity to a Klan rally into proof of membership, motive, or inherited ideology.
notes: Repair note: Replaced the populated medium text to remove unsupported claims of Klan membership and inherited political causation; corrected the unrelated immigration subcategory and topic tags.

title: Voice of America and USAGM Media Closure - International Broadcasting Propaganda Transformation
description_short: Voice of America and USAGM Media Closure - International Broadcasting Propaganda Transformation
notes: Needs context: The supplied source review found discussion of Project 2025 proposals to defund public media, including PBS and NPR, but no evidence that Trump eliminated USAGM or closed Voice of America, Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty, or Radio Free Asia. The original long description states these closures and a propaganda transformation as completed facts without support.

Proposed correction: Provide evidence of the specific USAGM or broadcaster closure and any editorial changes, or recast the entry around the proposals the cited sources actually discuss. The populated long description was cleared because its implementation claims were unsupported.

title: Trump asks FBI for protection in Atlantic City, help with investigations
description_short: Trump asks FBI for protection in Atlantic City, help with investigations
description_medium: FBI documents summarized by TrumpFile place agents in Donald Trump’s office in early April 1981 to discuss Atlantic City casinos and organized crime. Trump said he would cooperate if he entered the casino business, and later suggested using undercover agents at a casino. The FBI drafted a proposal and scheduled another meeting.
description_long: FBI records summarized by TrumpFile describe an April 1981 meeting between Donald Trump, two agents, and informant Daniel Sullivan, a labor consultant to Trump who owned Atlantic City property Trump wanted for a casino. The discussion concerned casino licensing and organized crime; Trump said he was wary of criminal elements and of the background scrutiny required to obtain a license. He told agents Damon Taylor and Walt Stowe that he would cooperate if he moved ahead in Atlantic City. At a June meeting, Trump said he wanted to cooperate during construction and after opening and suggested filling the casino with undercover agents. Taylor then contacted FBI offices to prepare an undercover proposal, which records describe as nearly complete before agents scheduled a third meeting for October 1. The documents establish discussions and planning, but not that the October meeting occurred, that the proposal was approved, or that undercover agents were deployed. They also do not document a request for personal protection, as the title suggests. The supported event is a prospective FBI cooperation plan connected to a possible casino, not a completed investigation.
notes: Needs context: The source supports meetings, Trump’s offer to cooperate if he pursued a casino, and an FBI undercover proposal that was scheduled for follow-up. It does not establish the title’s claim that Trump sought personal protection, that the plan was approved, or that the October 1 meeting occurred.
Proposed correction: Retitle the entry around the FBI discussions and proposed undercover plan, or provide a source documenting a request for protection and the proposal’s implementation.
Repair note: Replaced the non-specific topic tags with the FBI meeting, casino, organized-crime, and proposal subjects supported by the records.

notes: Needs context: The supplied synopsis and focused TrumpFile read do not identify a KGB contact or provide documentary evidence of direct coordination. title: Donald Trump retaliates against WSJ reporter for negative press
description_short: Donald Trump retaliates against WSJ reporter for negative press
description_medium: Trump offered Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Barsky and his family boxing tickets valued at $3,000, according to TrumpFile’s timeline. After Barsky published negative coverage of Trump’s finances, the timeline says a Trump spokesman accused him of extortion in a call to the New York Post. Barsky was moved off the Trump beat in June 1991.
description_long: TrumpFile’s timeline says Donald Trump offered Wall Street Journal reporter Neil Barsky and his family tickets to a major boxing match, valued at $3,000. Barsky wanted to decline, but his editor encouraged him to accept. Weeks later, after Barsky published a negative report on Trump’s finances, a Trump spokesman called a New York Post reporter and accused Barsky of extortion, claiming he had demanded favors in exchange for favorable coverage. The Post published that accusation. Trump then raised a conflict-of-interest complaint with Barsky’s editors, and the reporter was moved off the Trump beat in June 1991. The sequence is presented by the timeline as retaliation for critical coverage, but the available material does not independently establish Trump’s motive or prove that he directed the reassignment. The story concerns a valuable gift offer, a public accusation against a reporter, and a subsequent change in beat assignment. Those actions raise an ethics and press-freedom issue, while the causal account remains dependent on the source’s reported chronology.
notes: Needs context: TrumpFile’s timeline provides the gift, accusation, and beat reassignment sequence, but the linked New York Times article was inaccessible in this read. The material does not independently establish Trump’s retaliatory motive or that he directed the reassignment.
Proposed correction: Attribute the causal claim to the TrumpFile account and describe the reassignment as subsequent, or add contemporaneous reporting that establishes retaliation.

title: Federal Scientific Data Manipulation - Climate Research Falsification and Evidence Suppression
description_short: Federal Scientific Data Manipulation - Climate Research Falsification and Evidence Suppression
description_medium: The American Public Health Association’s overview of Project 2025 describes proposals to change the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s authority, structure, and data collection. The measures concern how public-health agencies would be organized and what information they gather; the page presents them as prospective recommendations in the blueprint.
subcategory: Federal Scientific Data Manipulation and Evidence Suppression
organization_tags: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention
notes: Needs context: APHA’s source describes proposed CDC authority, structure, and data-collection changes, not NOAA temperature-record alterations or EPA suppression of toxicity studies. The original long draft’s claims of systematic falsification and completed Trump administration actions are unsupported by the cited material.

Proposed correction: Identify a specific altered dataset or suppressed finding with documentation, or narrow the entry to APHA’s account of proposed CDC changes under Project 2025. The populated long description was cleared because it asserted unsupported completed acts.
Repair note: Replaced topic tags about unsubstantiated falsification with the Project 2025, CDC, and public-health-data subjects supported by the source.
